## Exams {#exams}

Two exams, each worth 25 points (about 5.6% of your grade). Delivery arrangements: ________. Complete each exam within its posted window: ________. Both are closed book, proctored, and
multiple choice.

Almost everything else you submit in this course is built with AI assistance, and that is
intended. These two sittings are the exception. They are the one place your own
understanding is measured on its own, which is why they exist and why they are worth
preparing for.

They are also deliberately low stakes. At about 5.6% each, the difference between a rough exam and
a strong one is about two percent of your course grade. That is enough to make preparing
worth it and not enough for one bad morning to matter.

### Midterm Exam {#midterm-exam}

**25 points | Week 3 | Window: ________ | Delivery: ________ | 36 questions**

Covers Weeks 1–3: the Agentic Workflow, Discovery, and Design axes. Scored the same way
as the final (below): 80% correct or better earns all 25 points.

### Final Exam {#final-exam}

**25 points | Week 7 | Window: ________ | Delivery: ________ | 84 questions, 2 hours**

Cumulative across all six axes. 72 questions count toward your score, weighted toward the axes
with the most to know: Agentic Workflow 16, Application Architecture 14, AI Systems 11, Discovery
11, Launch and Learn 11, and Design 9. The other 12 are trial questions being tested for future
exams; they look like the rest and do not count. Every question comes from what the chapters
teach, in three kinds: know it (what something is or is for), use it (which tool or step fits a
short situation), and predict it (what happens, or what went wrong, and why).

**Your points.** The exam is meant to be hard, so 80% correct earns full credit:
points = 25 × (your percent correct ÷ 80%), up to 25. For example, 80% or higher earns 25 points,
70% earns 21.9, and 60% earns 18.75.

**Your results by axis.** Alongside your score you get a result for each axis: Developing (below
50% on that axis), Proficient (50% to 79%), or Strong (80% and up). The exam measures what you know
on each axis, one part of your builder profile; your sprint work shows what you have built.

**The three kinds of questions.** Both exams use the same three kinds, in roughly equal numbers:

- **Know it** asks what something is or what it is for. Example: what does a leading indicator
  tell you that a lagging indicator does not?
- **Use it** gives you a short situation and asks which tool, step, or choice fits it. Example:
  which of these is a leading indicator for this product?
- **Predict it** describes a setup or a result and asks what will happen, or what went wrong and
  why. Example: the team watched this metric for a month; why did it fail to warn them?

Reading the chapters is the preparation; skimming them is not.

## Your builder profile {#builder-profile}

Your sprint reports include a builder profile: a six-sided chart with one area for each of the six
builder axes, each scored from 0 to 100. It shows what you can do, and it is not part of your grade.

- **Sprint work fills up to half of each area** (a quarter on AI Systems). It counts the concepts on
  that axis you have shown in your own work, and the depth level of that work, from following a
  template to changing the product because of what real users did.
- **The exams fill the rest.** The midterm tests three axes (Agentic Workflow, Discovery, and
  Design) and fills half of the exam part of those three, at the share of questions you got right.
  It shows as its own ring. The final fills the rest, on all six axes.
- **The starting center.** The center of the chart is your own rating from the opening self-assessment,
  counted on the part of each axis that no exam has measured yet. After the midterm it counts for
  half as much on the three axes the midterm tested.
- **Sprint rings never shrink.** Each sprint adds a ring outside the center for what that sprint
  showed. Once a ring is added, it stays.

## Sprints

Six sprints: Sprints 1–5 each occupy one week; Sprint 6 spans Weeks 6–7. Sprints 1 through 5 are worth 50 points. Sprint 6 is worth 100.
From Sprint 2 on, each sprint is two assignments in the course LMS: the **Plan** (10 points, deadline: ________) and the **Wrap-up** (40 points, or 90 for Sprint 6, due the day the sprint ends).

Every sprint is the same assignment: same structure, same deliverables, same rubric. What
changes is what you decide to work on. A sprint is a timebox, not a phase.

You are not all building the same kind of thing. Some of you are building your own product.
Some of you are on a team and are working on whatever your role covers. The requirements
below apply to both, and the rubric is the same for both.

### What you turn in, and how

Every sprint has the same four deliverables.

| Deliverable | What it is | Where it lives | How you turn it in | When | Points |
|---|---|---|---|---|--:|
| **Plan** | What you will do, why, how you will know it is done, and how hard you expect it to be. [`sprint-plan`](00-course-workflows.qmd#sprint-plan) helps you write it. | `sprints/sprint-N-plan.md` in your course repo | Commit it, and paste its GitHub link into **Sprint N Plan** in the course LMS. To change it later, run `sprint-plan` again; no resubmitting | Plan deadline: ________ | 10 |
| **Output** | What you finished this sprint, in whatever form the work takes: code, research, a design, a model, copy, a deck, an automation | Your course repo, another repo, a link, or your demo | Nothing separate to submit. List every place it lives under **Where the work lives** in your README | Wrap-up deadline: ________ | 20 |
| **Review** | What [`sprint-review`](00-course-workflows.qmd#sprint-review) produces: a report on your sprint, then your answers to its five retro questions | `sprints/sprint-N-review.md` in your course repo | Commit it, and paste its GitHub link into **Sprint N Wrap-up** in the course LMS | Wrap-up deadline: ________ | 10 |
| **Demo** | 2 to 3 minutes on Loom of the work, working | Loom | Paste the Loom share link into **Sprint N Wrap-up** in the course LMS. Set the Loom to "Anyone with the link" or share it with the course staff email (________) | Wrap-up deadline: ________ | 10 |

**Retro**, short for retrospective, is your part of the review: your answers to the five
questions `sprint-review` asks after it shows you the report. Did you hit the goal, about how
many hours did you work, why did the plan change if it did, how hard was it really, and what will you
change next sprint. It saves your answers word for word with the report.

Sprint 6 is worth 100: Plan 10, Output 50, Review 20, Demo 20, and it wraps up in Week 7; exact deadline: ________.

### How every sprint works

Two local workflows support every sprint: [sprint-plan](00-course-workflows.qmd#sprint-plan) at the start and [sprint-review](00-course-workflows.qmd#sprint-review) at the end. Use Codex (primary) or Claude (alternative). Both read the same files in your starter repo's `course-prompts/` folder. Paste the plain-text prompts on the workflow page; no slash-command installation or external template update is required.

#### Day one

Run [`sprint-plan`](00-course-workflows.qmd#sprint-plan). It asks you what you are going to do and writes `sprints/sprint-N-plan.md`:

```markdown
# Sprint N Plan

**Goal:** What will be true by the end of this sprint that is not true now?

**Why this:** Why is this the right next thing?

**Done looks like:** How will you know the goal was met? Be specific enough
that someone else could check.

**Predicted difficulty:** 1 to 5.
```

**Submit it in the course LMS by the posted plan deadline (________).** Commit and push the file, then paste its GitHub
link into that sprint's Plan assignment. On time, with Goal, Why this, Done looks like, and
Predicted difficulty all filled in, earns all 10 points. You do not resubmit when the plan
changes: the link always shows the current file.

**You can change the plan.** Plans change once you learn something, and that is normal. To change
yours, run `sprint-plan` again during the sprint. It asks what is changing and why, updates the
plan, adds a dated note like this one, and commits it:

```markdown
**Changes:** Mar 3: dropped the slide template and added a competitor benchmark, because the
licensing research had to come first.
```

There is nothing to resubmit in the course LMS: your plan link always shows the current file. Changes
cost nothing. At the end, your work is read against the plan as it stands, and your
retro says how it changed. A change with no note is the one thing to avoid: without it, nobody
reading your plan can tell what you set out to do.

[]{#the-two-weeks}

#### During the sprint

Do the work, in your repo.

#### Wrap-up deadline: ________

**1. Run [sprint-review](00-course-workflows.qmd#sprint-review).** Confirm the sprint window and which projects belong to this sprint. The agent reads only the projects and evidence you authorize. It uses your plan, commits, artifacts, and any session notes you choose to provide to report when you worked, where you got stuck and how you got unstuck, what took the most time, and which of the six axes your work advanced. Missing evidence is marked unknown. Private source code and raw session transcripts do not go in the report.

**2. Answer its five retro questions.** After showing you the report, `sprint-review` asks:

1. Did you hit the goal? Yes, partly, or no, and why.
2. How many hours do you estimate you worked on this sprint, all in, including time away from your coding agent?
3. If the plan changed, why?
4. Actual difficulty, 1 to 5, and why it differed from what you predicted.
5. What will you change next sprint?

Answer in your own words. It saves your answers exactly as you write them at the bottom of
`sprints/sprint-N-review.md`, then helps you review, commit, and push the file to your own repo.

**3. Record a 2 to 3 minute demo on [Loom](https://www.loom.com).** Show your work, working, with real content, as
described in [What your demo shows](#what-your-demo-shows). No intro and no reflection: the actual work. Loom only: not Google Drive, YouTube, or an uploaded
file. Submit the Loom share link. A demo that is not a Loom scores 0. **Make sure Professor Teigen can see your video: in Loom's Share settings, set it to "Anyone with the
link" or share it with the course staff email (________).** A video the course staff cannot open is not graded until it is shared.

**4. Submit two links in that sprint's Wrap-up assignment in the course LMS:** your review file on
GitHub (`sprints/sprint-N-review.md`, with your retro at the bottom) and your Loom demo. Before
you do, make sure the **Where the work lives** section of your README lists every repo and live
link someone would need to check your output. For Sprint 1, also include your course repo URL.

### What you have to have

- **Output.** Something real and finished exists now that did not at the sprint start. It does not
  have to be public, launched, or used by anyone: plenty of valuable work is never shown to
  anyone else.
- **Professor Teigen can check it, privately.** It is in your course repo, in another repo shared with
  Professor Teigen or summarized by `sprint-review`, at a link, or shown working in your demo.
  Work nobody can check, anywhere, cannot be graded.
- **The plan,** submitted in the course LMS by the posted plan deadline (________), committed, and kept current with any changes
  noted.
- **The review,** committed: the `sprint-review` report with your answers to its five retro
  questions at the bottom.
- **The Loom demo, 2 to 3 minutes.**

### What output means for different work

Output is whatever your sprint produced, on any of the six axes. Code is one kind among many.
What counts is that it is real, finished for this sprint, and checkable by the course.

| If your sprint was | Output means |
|---|---|
| A product feature | It works, in your repo or deployed, and your demo shows it working |
| Frontend or design work | The interface or the designs exist, not just a description of them |
| A landing page or campaign | The page or campaign is built, published or ready to publish |
| Pricing or financial modeling | The model exists and runs on real numbers |
| Marketing or sales copy | The copy is written and finished, not an outline |
| An automation or workflow | It runs, and your demo shows it running |
| Research or discovery | The findings are written up, with what you concluded from them |
| Selling or outreach | The asks are made and on record: who you asked, when, what you asked for, and what they said |
| Recruiting partners, customers, or payers | The same: graded on the asks you made and can show (see [Goals that need someone else to say yes](#grading-rubric)) |
| Analytics or measurement | The tracking is set up and returning real data |

If your work does not fit any of these, say what output means for it in your plan file before
the sprint starts.

### What your demo shows

"Working" in the Demo rubric depends on the kind of work. Show the work itself, opened, for
most of the video.

| If your sprint was | Your demo shows |
|---|---|
| A product feature | The feature in use: click through it |
| Frontend or design work | The interface or designs, clicked or scrolled through |
| A landing page or campaign | The page live, with its sign-up or checkout used |
| Pricing or financial modeling | The model, with one input changed and the result it gives |
| Marketing or sales copy | The finished copy, where it will run |
| An automation or workflow | It running, start to finish |
| Research or discovery | One or two of your notes opened, and what you concluded |
| Selling or outreach | Your deck, the asks you sent, and your pipeline |
| Analytics or measurement | The dashboard returning real data |

Keep real names, emails, and phone numbers off the screen. Open the copies in your repo, with
names removed, instead of the original notes or your CRM.

#### Any real artifact counts as output

Your sprint can advance any of the six axes, and every one produces artifacts. Code is one kind
among many. Any digital artifact that reflects real work counts, in whatever format it
naturally takes:

| Axis | Artifacts that count, for example |
|---|---|
| Agentic Workflow | An `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`, reusable prompts and skills, subagent setups, an automation that runs, prompts and tool use in the product, an eval set and its results |
| Discovery | Interview notes and synthesis, personas, a problem statement, survey results, a competitive teardown |
| Design | Flows, wireframes and mockups, a Figma file, a usability test write-up, a live interface, a spec with user stories and acceptance criteria |
| Application Architecture | Code, a deployed app on Vercel or elsewhere, a data model, an API, tests, a working model call or retrieval pipeline |
| AI Systems | A write-up of how your model behaves and why, a hallucination or failure analysis, a retrieval or context-window experiment and what it showed |
| Launch and Learn | A landing page, a pitch deck, pricing or a financial model, sales copy, an analytics dashboard |

Markdown files, Word documents, slide decks, spreadsheets, PDFs, images, and live links are all
fine. Two tests apply to every one of them: it is real work (not a template or a placeholder),
and the course can check it. It does not have to be public. Commit it to a repo or list it under
**Where the work lives** in your README; for a Google Doc, Figma file, or anything else behind a
link, make sure it opens for us (set it to "Anyone with the link can view" or share it with
the course staff email (________)).

Interview notes and recordings are about real people. Commit notes and synthesis with names
removed, and keep recordings out of the repo.

### The difficulty scale

| | |
|---|---|
| **1** | I already know how to do this |
| **2** | I know most of it, with a few small gaps to fill |
| **3** | I will have to learn something new, but the path is clear |
| **4** | I will have to learn a lot, and the path is not clear |
| **5** | I do not know whether this is possible |

Difficulty is not graded in either direction. Rate it honestly.

### Grading rubric

50 points, or 100 for Sprint 6. The same four categories every sprint. The Plan assignment is
the first category; the Wrap-up assignment is the other three.

| Category | Points | Sprint 6 | What earns full points |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| **Plan** | 10 | 10 | Its GitHub link submitted in the course LMS by the posted plan deadline (________), with Goal, Why this, Done looks like, and Predicted difficulty all filled in. Graded for completion. |
| **Output** | 20 | 50 | Real, finished, and checkable by the course; it does not have to be public or used by anyone. Read against your plan as it stands at the end, and weighed by how hard the work was for you. A goal that needs someone else's yes is graded on the asks you made. |
| **Review** | 10 | 20 | Report committed, with your retro answering all five questions. Each question left unanswered costs 1 point. An empty retro earns at most half. Your hours estimate is never graded on the number. |
| **Demo** | 10 | 20 | 2 to 3 minutes on Loom of your work, working, as described in [What your demo shows](#what-your-demo-shows), with real content. A demo that is not a Loom scores 0. Set it to "Anyone with the link" or share it with the course staff email (________). Length rules below. |

**Demo length.** Aim for 2 to 3 minutes. A demo up to 3:30 loses no points. From Sprint 3, each started
30 seconds past 3:30 costs 1 point (3:31 to 4:00 is minus 1, 4:01 to 4:30 minus 2, 4:31 to 5:00 minus 3).
Sprint 6 aims for 3 to 4 minutes, and the same scale starts past 4:30.

The plan is graded for completion, and your predicted difficulty is not graded. Aim high.
From Sprint 2 on, output is weighed by how hard the work actually was for you, judged from
the work itself: an ambitious goal you partly reach and
account for in your retro can still earn full points.

**Goals that need someone else to say yes.** Some goals depend on other people: signing design
partners, getting a customer to pay, reaching a number of signups. You control the asks; you do
not control the answers. For these goals, Output is graded on the asks you made and can show:
who you asked, when, what you asked for, and what they said. A no, or a "not yet," costs no
points when the ask is on record and your retro says what you learned from it. When you plan
one of these goals, write the asks into it, for example "Ask 10 contractors to be design
partners, and sign 2."

**Disputing a deduction.** From Sprint 3, your sprint report lists each point deducted, with the rule behind it. If you think one is wrong, identify the deduction and provide links, screenshots, or notes. Disputes remain open for one week after grades are released. Professor Teigen reviews the deduction against the rubric, so your score can rise, stay the same, or fall. Submission channel and link: ________.

**Sprints 1 and 2, and other questions about sprint feedback:** identify the part of the report and explain what you think was missed. Course feedback channel and link: ________.

### Confidential company work

Many of you build inside a company whose code, data, or customers are not yours alone to share.
You never have to share a company repo. Any of these works:

- Share the repo with Professor Teigen (GitHub username: ________) if you and your
  team are comfortable with that. Your course repo can stay private either way.
- Leave it unshared and list it under **Where the work lives** in your README. `sprint-review`
  reads its commit history on your own computer and puts a summary in your report: dates,
  messages, and file names, never code.
- Show the result instead: the live product, a store listing, an account for the graders, or
  your Loom. For most work that is the strongest evidence anyway.
- If none of that works, build a sanitized version with fake data and note it in your plan file.

Nothing in this course has to be public.

## Peer Assignment

The peer assignment teaches you to give and receive constructive feedback, a critical professional skill. You'll be randomly paired with a classmate.

---

### Peer Product Testing {#peer-product-testing}

**50 points | Assigned Week 6; completed Week 7 | Deadline: ________**

**Goal:** Be a real test user for a peer's product and provide actionable UX feedback.

**Process:**

1. You'll be assigned a partner
2. You become an actual user of their product
3. You sign up, use core features, and try to break things
4. You record the whole thing

**Deliverable:** A 5-minute Loom video of you using your peer's product. That's it.

**How to record your test session:**

1. **Start Loom, share your screen, and open their app URL**
2. **Think out loud the entire time:** narrate what you see, what you expect, where you're confused, what works
3. **Try to complete the core task:** sign up, use the main feature, see if your data persists
4. **Try to break things:** what happens with bad input? Edge cases? Unexpected flows?
5. **End with your summary:** look at the camera and give:
   - 3 things that worked well (be specific)
   - 3 things you'd improve (most impactful first)
   - Would you use this product? Why or why not?

**Submit:** Your Loom URL in the course LMS. Share the video with your peer too; it is useful feedback for them.

**Grading Rubric (50 points)**

| Score | What the TA sees |
|-------|-----------------|
| **45-50** | Genuine engagement: spent real time exploring the product. Think-aloud narration is specific and continuous. Summary feedback is actionable and constructive. |
| **35-44** | Good test session but narration is sparse, or summary feedback is vague. Clearly used the product but didn't explore it in depth. |
| **25-34** | Surface-level engagement. Quick walkthrough without much exploration or thoughtful feedback. |
| **15-24** | Video submitted but minimal effort. Barely used the product. |
| **0** | Not submitted. |

::: {.callout-tip title="Testing Mindset"}
Your job is to help your peer see their product the way a new user sees it. Be honest but kind. The best feedback is specific ("The button on the checkout page didn't respond when I clicked it") not vague ("The checkout was buggy").
:::
